items.q: According to Sommerville, "software" is best defined as:
options: Computer programs and all associated documentation and configuration data
The hardware plus the operating system
The user interface and its design
items.explain: Software = programs + associated documentation + configuration data needed to make the programs work correctly. It is not just code.

items.q: The term "software engineering" was first coined at the:
items.explain: It was coined at the 1968 NATO Software Engineering Conference (Garmisch) in response to the 'software crisis'.

items.q: Which is NOT one of Sommerville's four essential attributes of good software?
items.explain: The four are maintainability, dependability & security, efficiency, and acceptability. Minimising lines of code is not a quality attribute.

items.q: A bespoke (customised) software product differs from a generic product in that:
options: It is always free to use
Its specification is controlled by a specific customer who commissioned it
It cannot be sold on the open market because it is illegal
items.explain: Bespoke/customised products are commissioned by a specific customer who owns/controls the specification; generic products are sold to anyone and the developer controls the spec.

items.q: The July 2024 CrowdStrike global outage was fundamentally caused by:
options: A faulty content/configuration update that crashed the Windows kernel
A hardware defect in Intel CPUs
items.explain: It was a quality/process failure: a defective channel-file update caused an out-of-bounds read in a kernel-level driver, producing BSODs worldwide. It was not a cyber-attack.

items.q: Which deployment practice would most directly have limited the blast radius of the CrowdStrike update?
options: Staged / canary rollout instead of pushing to all machines at once
items.explain: A staged/canary rollout releases to a small ring first and watches for problems before widening — containing the blast radius. The update instead went to everyone simultaneously.

items.q: Which four fundamental activities are common to every software process?
items.explain: Every process includes specification (define what), development (design & implement), validation (check it), and evolution (change it).

items.q: The waterfall model is most appropriate when:
options: Requirements change frequently and are poorly understood
Requirements are stable and well-understood up front
The customer wants to see working software every two weeks
Risk must be re-assessed every iteration
items.explain: Waterfall is rigid and document-driven; it suits projects where requirements are stable and well-understood. It handles change poorly.

items.q: In the V-model, the test level paired with the 'architectural/system design' phase is:
items.explain: The V-model pairs each build phase with a test level: requirements↔acceptance, system design↔system testing, architectural design↔integration testing, module design↔unit testing.

items.q: The distinguishing feature of Boehm's Spiral model is:
options: Explicit, iterative risk assessment and resolution in every loop
It delivers the entire system only at the very end
items.explain: Each spiral loop has four quadrants, and the defining one is identifying & resolving risks. Risk is explicitly assessed and resolved throughout the process.

items.q: The key difference between incremental and iterative development is:
options: Incremental delivers the system in usable slices; iterative builds a rough whole then refines it repeatedly
items.explain: Incremental = deliver complete slices of functionality over time; iterative = build a version of the whole then refine over passes. Agile is both.

items.q: The Secure SDLC (SecDLC) is built around the principle of:
options: Adding security only as a final penetration test
Shifting security left — building it into every phase
Outsourcing all security to a third party
items.explain: The SecDLC weaves security into every phase (Investigation, Analysis, Design, Implementation, Maintenance) — 'shifting security left' so flaws are caught early.

items.q: Pressman's '4 Ps' of software project management, in order, are:
items.explain: People → Product → Process → Project. People are the most important asset; the others build on them. (Don't confuse with the marketing 4 Ps.)

items.q: Which of the 4 Ps does Pressman identify as the most important?
items.explain: People are the most important asset — software is built by people for people; staffing, skills and communication dominate success.

items.q: Which is one of the four values of the Agile Manifesto?
options: Following a plan over responding to change
items.explain: The four values prefer the LEFT: individuals & interactions > processes/tools; working software > documentation; customer collaboration > contract negotiation; responding to change > following a plan.

items.q: In Scrum, who is responsible for prioritising the Product Backlog?
items.explain: The Product Owner owns and prioritises the Product Backlog and represents the customer/business — deciding what gets built and in what order.

items.q: The Scrum Master is best described as a:
options: Boss who assigns tasks to developers
items.explain: The Scrum Master is a servant-leader/facilitator — coaching the team, removing impediments, and ensuring the process is followed. They do NOT assign work like a traditional manager.

items.q: Which Scrum ceremony focuses on inspecting the TEAM and PROCESS (not the product)?
items.explain: The Sprint Retrospective inspects the team/process (what went well, what to improve). The Sprint Review inspects the product (demo the increment).

items.q: The standard user-story template is:
options: As a <user>, I want <goal>, so that <benefit>
items.explain: 'As a <type of user>, I want <some goal>, so that <reason/benefit>' captures who, what and why. (Given/When/Then is the format for acceptance criteria.)

items.q: In the INVEST criteria for a good user story, the 'I' and 'S' stand for:
items.explain: INVEST = Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable. 'I'=Independent, 'S'=Small (fits in one sprint).

items.q: In Extreme Programming, writing a failing test BEFORE writing the code is called:
items.explain: TDD = write the (failing) test first, then write code until it passes. Refactoring improves structure without changing behaviour; pair programming is two devs at one machine.

items.q: Refactoring is defined as:
options: Improving the internal structure of code without changing its external behaviour
Rewriting the program in a new language
items.explain: Refactoring changes internal structure while preserving external behaviour. If behaviour changes, it is not refactoring.

items.q: The four activities of the requirements engineering process are:
items.explain: RE = elicitation (discovery), analysis & negotiation, specification (documentation/SRS), and validation — often with requirements management as an ongoing fifth.

items.q: Which elicitation technique is PASSIVE?
items.explain: Ethnography/observation is passive — the analyst observes real work without steering it. Interviews, workshops and brainstorming are active (analyst-driven).

items.q: User requirements differ from system requirements in that user requirements are:
options: Abstract natural-language statements aimed at customers
items.explain: User requirements are abstract natural-language statements for customers/users; system requirements are detailed, structured specifications for developers.

items.q: "The system shall respond to any search query within 2 seconds" is an example of a:
items.explain: It constrains HOW WELL the system performs (response time) rather than WHAT service it provides — a non-functional performance requirement.

items.q: In Sommerville's NFR taxonomy, a requirement that 'the software must be implemented in Java' is a(n):
items.explain: A requirement derived from the developing organisation's policies/standards (e.g. mandated language/process) is an Organisational (development) requirement.

items.q: Why are non-functional requirements often considered more critical than functional ones?
options: A single failed NFR can make the entire system unusable even if all features work
They never conflict with each other
They do not need to be tested
items.explain: NFRs typically apply to the system as a whole; failing one (e.g. security, performance) can render the whole system unusable even when every feature is present.

items.q: The CIA triad in security stands for:
items.explain: CIA = Confidentiality (disclosure only to authorised), Integrity (no unauthorised modification), Availability (accessible when needed).

items.q: When writing security requirements, the 'SMART' criteria require each to be:
items.explain: SMART = Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. (INVEST is for user stories — don't swap them.)

items.q: The SRS document is best described as:
options: A design document describing how to code the system
The agreed contract stating what the team should implement
items.explain: The SRS is the official agreed statement of WHAT to implement (user + system requirements) — the contract between customer and developer. It says what, not how.

items.q: The primary purpose of a Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM) is to:
options: Map each requirement forward to design/code/tests (and back) to ensure coverage
items.explain: The RTM traces every requirement to its design, code and test cases (forward) and traces artifacts back to requirements (backward) — proving coverage and enabling change-impact analysis.

items.q: A UML class diagram is classified as a:
items.explain: Class, object, component and deployment diagrams are structural (static). Use-case, sequence, activity and state diagrams are behavioural (dynamic).

items.q: In a use-case diagram, the «include» relationship means the included use case is:
options: Always executed as part of the base use case
items.explain: «include» = mandatory/always (reusable common behaviour). «extend» = optional/conditional. Mnemonic: include='always', extend='sometimes'.

items.q: In use-case modelling, an 'actor' is:
options: A role external to the system — a user or another system — that interacts with it
items.explain: An actor is a ROLE external to the system; it can be a human role or another system (e.g. a payment gateway). One person may play several actors.

items.q: A persona in requirements engineering is:
options: A real named customer who signs the contract
A fictional but research-based character representing a key user type
A use-case actor with a UML stereotype
items.explain: A persona is a fictional, realistic archetype of a user type (with goals, frustrations, context) used to keep design user-centred and fight the 'elastic user' problem.

items.q: Ethnography is especially good at uncovering:
options: Tacit/implicit requirements that users never think to state
items.explain: By observing real work in context, ethnography surfaces tacit 'how we really do it' knowledge that interviews miss — e.g. the distrust of online payment that drove Cash-on-Delivery.

items.q: Boehm's distinction: 'Are we building the product right?' refers to ___, and 'Are we building the right product?' refers to ___.
items.explain: Verification = building the product right (conforms to spec). Validation = building the right product (meets user needs).

items.q: Order the terminology chain correctly:
options: Error (human mistake) → defect/fault in code → failure at runtime
items.explain: A human commits an ERROR, which introduces a DEFECT/FAULT (bug) in the code, which when executed may cause a FAILURE. A defect does not always cause a failure.

items.q: Testing the interfaces between combined modules is called:
items.explain: Integration testing checks the interactions/interfaces between modules. Unit = one component; system = the whole integrated system; acceptance = against customer needs.

items.q: Black-box testing designs test cases based on:
options: The internal code structure and paths
The specification (inputs and expected outputs), without seeing the code
items.explain: Black-box (functional) testing uses the spec — inputs→expected outputs — without knowledge of the code. White-box uses internal structure (e.g. branch coverage).

items.q: Without which field can a test case not distinguish pass from fail?
items.explain: The predefined expected result (oracle) is what 'actual result' is compared against. Without it you cannot judge pass/fail.

items.q: Defect density is calculated as:
options: Number of testers ÷ number of modules
Number of defects ÷ size (e.g. per KLOC or function point)
items.explain: Defect density = defects / size (per 1000 lines of code, KLOC, or per function point). Normalising by size lets you compare quality across modules/releases.

items.q: Achieving 100% statement coverage guarantees that:
options: Every statement was executed at least once — but outputs may still be wrong and code may be missing
items.explain: Coverage tells you what code ran, not whether outputs were correct or whether required code is missing. 100% statement coverage ≠ bug-free; branch coverage is stronger.

items.q: Penetration testing and fuzzing are activities found in:
items.explain: Security validation adds misuse cases, penetration testing, vulnerability scanning and fuzzing on top of normal V&V — asking 'can it be made to do what it shouldn't?'.
